Graphs where only one pair's shortest path is needed

cards.prompt: Johnson's ___ every edge using vertex potentials h(v) computed by one Bellman-Ford run from an added source vertex connected to all others with zero-weight edges: the new weight is w'(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(u) - h(v), where h(v) is the shortest distance from that added source to v.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 23 (All-Pairs Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: What must be true of h(v) for Johnson's reweighting formula w'(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(u) - h(v) to guarantee every reweighted edge is non-negative?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 23 (All-Pairs Shortest Paths)
cards.answer: h(v) must satisfy the triangle inequality h(v) <= h(u) + w(u, v) for every edge (u, v) — which is exactly the property Bellman-Ford's shortest-distance values from the added source guarantee, since a shortest distance to v can never exceed a shortest distance to u plus the direct edge weight from u to v.

cards.prompt: Explain why Johnson's reweighting preserves *which* path is shortest between any two vertices, even though it changes every individual edge's weight — what does the h(u) - h(v) telescoping do to a path's total reweighted length compared to its original length?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 23 (All-Pairs Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Once reweighted, Johnson's runs Dijkstra from every vertex on the non-negative graph and converts distances back by reversing the potential shift, for a total running time of ___ with a Fibonacci-heap Dijkstra — asymptotically better than Floyd-Warshall's Theta(V^3) when E is small relative to V^2.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 23 (All-Pairs Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: BFS colors vertices white (undiscovered), gray (discovered, frontier), and black (finished), and maintains a distance d[v] and a predecessor pi[v] for each vertex. It processes gray vertices in the order they were discovered, using a ___. On each step it dequeues a vertex u, and for each white neighbor v, sets d[v] = d[u] + 1, pi[v] = u, colors v gray, and enqueues it; once u's whole adjacency list has been scanned this way, u is colored black.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Why must BFS use a FIFO queue rather than, say, a stack, for the distances it computes to be correct?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: A FIFO queue guarantees vertices are dequeued in the same order they were enqueued — non-decreasing order of discovery, hence non-decreasing distance from s — so every vertex at distance k is fully processed (and every distance-(k+1) neighbor discovered) before any distance-(k+1) vertex is dequeued. A stack would process the most recently discovered vertex next, exploring depth-first instead of by distance, and d[v] would no longer equal the true shortest-path distance.

cards.prompt: The predecessor pointers pi[v] set during the search form the ___, rooted at s: it contains exactly one path from s to each reachable vertex, and that path is a shortest path in the original graph.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: In an unweighted graph, what does d[v] equal after running BFS from s?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

choices.text: The number of edges on a shortest path from s to v
The number of edges on some path from s to v, not necessarily shortest
The total number of vertices visited before v
The depth of v in a depth-first search tree rooted at s

cards.prompt: This shortest-path guarantee is specific to ___ graphs, where every edge contributes the same cost of 1 to a path's length; BFS's distances have no meaning as shortest-path lengths once edges carry different weights, which is why weighted shortest paths need Dijkstra's algorithm or Bellman-Ford instead.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: What does the BFS tree rooted at s represent, and what specific property does its s-to-v path have in the original graph?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: It is the tree formed by the predecessor pointers pi[v] set during the search; the tree's s-to-v path is a shortest path from s to v in the original graph, measured in number of edges.

cards.prompt: BFS discovers vertices in "waves" ordered by distance from the source. Explain why this wave structure is precisely what guarantees each vertex's first-discovered distance is its true shortest-path distance, and would break if a vertex could be discovered a second time at a smaller distance.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Running time is ___: each vertex is enqueued and dequeued at most once (Theta(V)), and each vertex's adjacency list is scanned exactly once across the whole run (Theta(E)).
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Each vertex gets a ___ d[v], set when it is first colored gray. It also gets a finish time f[v], set when its adjacency list is fully explored and it is colored black — DFS-VISIT recurses into every white neighbor before returning, so d[u] < f[u] always, and because DFS is recursive these timestamps nest.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: The ___ states that for any two vertices u and v, exactly one of three relationships holds between their intervals [d[u], f[u]] and [d[v], f[v]]: the intervals are entirely disjoint, or one is entirely contained within the other — nested, like well-formed parentheses — but they can never partially overlap.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: According to the parenthesis theorem, if [d[u], f[u]] and [d[v], f[v]] overlap at all, what must be true?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

choices.text: One interval is entirely nested inside the other
Exactly one of d[v] or f[v] falls inside [d[u], f[u]]
u and v must be adjacent in G
The two intervals must be identical

cards.prompt: Why can two vertices' discovery/finish intervals never partially overlap in a DFS?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: DFS-VISIT(v) only ever runs entirely inside the call to DFS-VISIT(u) that discovered it, or entirely after u has already finished — a recursive call cannot start inside u's interval and finish after it, since u's own call cannot return until every recursive call it made has returned. That call-stack structure forces disjoint-or-nested, never partial overlap.

cards.prompt: The ___ says v is a descendant of u in the depth-first forest if and only if, at the time u is discovered, there is a path from u to v consisting entirely of white vertices.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: DFS classifies every edge (u, v) into one of four kinds relative to the depth-first forest it produces. A *tree edge* is one by which v was discovered. A ___ connects u to an ancestor v, pointing "up" the tree — and it is exactly this kind of edge whose presence signals a cycle in a directed graph. A *forward edge* connects u to a descendant v that is not a tree edge. A *cross edge* is everything else: no ancestor/descendant relationship holds between u and v in either direction. All four kinds arise only in a directed graph: a DFS of an undirected graph produces tree and back edges only, since an undirected edge is explored from whichever endpoint DFS reaches first and so can never point forward to an already-finished descendant or sideways to an unrelated vertex.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: What does the white-path theorem say about vertex v being a descendant of u in the depth-first forest?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: v is a descendant of u if and only if, at the moment u is discovered, v is reachable from u along a path made entirely of vertices that are still white at that instant.

cards.prompt: Explain why a directed graph contains a cycle if and only if a DFS of it produces at least one back edge — what does a back edge (u, v) mean about the relationship between u and v, and how does that force a cycle?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Running time is ___, the same bound as BFS: Theta(V) to initialize and visit every vertex once, plus Theta(E) to scan every adjacency list exactly once across all recursive calls combined.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm maintains a set S of vertices whose final shortest distance is already known, and repeatedly moves the ___ vertex u outside S into S, relaxing all of u's outgoing edges.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail if the graph contains a negative-weight edge, specifically in terms of what "finalizing" a vertex means?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)
cards.answer: Dijkstra permanently fixes d[u] the moment u is extracted from the queue and never relaxes into u again afterward. With a negative edge, a vertex v added to S later — with a larger d[v] at the time it was extracted — can have an outgoing negative edge to u that would lower d[u] below its already-finalized value. Because u is never revisited, that improvement is silently missed, and Dijkstra's finalized d[u] is not just imprecise but can be wrong.

cards.prompt: Which best describes the actual mechanism by which a negative edge breaks Dijkstra's correctness?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

choices.text: A vertex is finalized (permanently removed from consideration) based on distances that a later, negative-weight relaxation could still have improved, and Dijkstra never revisits finalized vertices
Negative weights make the priority queue's comparisons undefined
Dijkstra's algorithm cannot represent negative numbers in its distance array
Negative weights cause the algorithm to loop forever

cards.prompt: Dijkstra's running time depends on the priority queue exactly as Prim's does: ___ with a binary heap, or O(E + V lg V) with a Fibonacci heap.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: A ___ admits a much simpler and faster algorithm precisely because it has a topological order: sort the vertices topologically, then relax every vertex's outgoing edges exactly once, in that order — every d[v] is final the first time v is reached, because no edge ever points backward in a topological order.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Why does processing vertices in topological order make one relaxation pass over each vertex's edges sufficient, even with negative edges present?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)
cards.answer: In topological order, by the time vertex u is processed, every edge into u has already been relaxed (all of u's predecessors come earlier in the order), so d[u] is already final; relaxing u's own outgoing edges then can only need to happen once, since no later vertex can have an edge back into u to improve it further.

cards.prompt: This algorithm tolerates negative weights (unlike Dijkstra's) because it never "finalizes" a vertex based on a greedy minimality argument — it runs in ___, the topological sort's cost plus one pass of relaxation.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Explain why the DAG shortest-paths algorithm's tolerance for negative weights does not contradict Bellman-Ford's need for |V| - 1 rounds to handle negative weights correctly — what extra structural guarantee does a DAG's topological order supply that a general graph lacks?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: An ___ represents a graph G = (V, E) as an array of |V| lists, one per vertex, where each list holds that vertex's neighbors (or, for a weighted graph, neighbor-plus-weight pairs). Its space usage is Theta(V + E), growing with the number of edges actually present.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: An adjacency list represents a graph G = (V, E) as an array of |V| lists, one per vertex, where each list holds that vertex's neighbors (or, for a weighted graph, neighbor-plus-weight pairs). Its space usage is ___, growing with the number of edges actually present.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: An adjacency matrix is a |V| x |V| array where entry (u, v) records whether edge (u, v) exists (and its weight, if any). Its space usage is ___, regardless of how many edges exist.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: A graph has 10,000 vertices and 15,000 edges. Which representation uses asymptotically less space?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

choices.text: Adjacency list — Theta(V + E) versus Theta(V^2) for the matrix
Adjacency matrix — Theta(V^2) versus Theta(V + E) for the list
Both use the same asymptotic space for any graph
It depends on whether the graph is directed

cards.prompt: The tradeoff is symmetric with query time. Listing a vertex's neighbors takes time proportional to its ___ with an adjacency list, but Theta(V) with a matrix, since you must scan an entire row regardless of how many neighbors actually exist. Conversely, testing whether a specific edge (u, v) exists is Theta(1) with a matrix — one array lookup — but can take up to O(V) with a list, since you may have to scan the whole neighbor list of u to find (or rule out) v.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: The tradeoff is symmetric with query time. Listing a vertex's neighbors takes time proportional to its degree with an adjacency list, but Theta(V) with a matrix, since you must scan an entire row regardless of how many neighbors actually exist. Conversely, testing whether a specific edge (u, v) exists is ___ with a matrix — one array lookup — but can take up to O(V) with a list, since you may have to scan the whole neighbor list of u to find (or rule out) v.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Why can testing for a specific edge be slower with an adjacency list than with a matrix, even though listing all of a vertex's neighbors is faster?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: An adjacency list only stores edges that exist, so finding one specific edge (u, v) means scanning u's neighbor list until v turns up or the list ends — up to Theta(degree(u)) work. A matrix trades that away for Theta(1) lookup of any single edge, at the cost of Theta(V) to enumerate only the neighbors that actually exist.

cards.prompt: A graph is dense enough that |E| is close to |V^2| (e.g., a nearly complete graph). Explain whether the space and query-time case for adjacency lists still holds, and why a matrix representation becomes more attractive as a graph gets denser.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: ___ sorts all edges by weight and considers them one at a time, adding an edge if its two endpoints are in different components of the forest built so far, and skipping it otherwise since adding it would form a cycle.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: It uses a disjoint-set data structure to test "are u and v already connected?" and to merge components. With union by rank and path compression, a sequence of m operations on n elements takes ___ total, essentially constant time per operation.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: Why is testing "are u and v in the same component?" via disjoint sets the right operation to avoid creating a cycle, rather than, say, checking whether v is already in the tree?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)
cards.answer: Kruskal's builds a forest, not a single growing tree, so "already connected" is the relevant notion of cycle risk, not "already visited" — two vertices can each be in the tree without being connected to each other yet, and adding an edge between two already-connected vertices is exactly what closes a cycle, regardless of whether both endpoints have been seen before.

cards.prompt: ___ instead grows a single tree from an arbitrary root, repeatedly adding the minimum-weight edge connecting the current tree to a vertex outside it — exactly the cut property applied to the cut between the tree so far and everything else.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: Prim's algorithm's running time depends on which choice?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

choices.text: The priority-queue implementation used for EXTRACT-MIN and DECREASE-KEY
Whether the graph is sorted by weight beforehand
Whether a disjoint-set structure is used instead of a queue
The order in which the root vertex's neighbors are listed

cards.prompt: With a ___, each EXTRACT-MIN and DECREASE-KEY costs O(lg V), giving Prim's a total running time of O(E lg V).
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: With a Fibonacci heap, DECREASE-KEY drops to O(1) amortized, giving a total of ___ — asymptotically better on dense graphs, where E dominates the E lg V term of the binary-heap version.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: What two priority-queue implementations give Prim's algorithm its two standard running times, and what are those running times?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)
cards.answer: A binary heap gives O(E lg V); a Fibonacci heap gives O(E + V lg V).

cards.prompt: Explain why Prim's, unlike Kruskal's, needs the graph to be connected as an explicit precondition for the single-tree-growth strategy to visit every vertex, and what result you get from Prim's if you run it on a disconnected graph.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: Given a flow network G with capacities c(u, v), the ___ Gf has, for each edge (u, v), a residual capacity cf(u, v) = c(u, v) - f(u, v) in the forward direction, and a residual capacity cf(v, u) = f(u, v) in the reverse direction — representing the option to "undo" flow already sent along (u, v).
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)

cards.prompt: An ___ is a simple path from s to t in the residual network; the maximum amount of additional flow it can carry is the minimum residual capacity of any edge along it, called its residual capacity.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)

cards.prompt: Why does the residual network need a reverse edge with capacity f(u, v), given that the original graph may not have had an edge (v, u) at all?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)
cards.answer: An augmenting path is allowed to route flow backward across an edge that already carries flow, effectively canceling some of it, which lets a later augmenting step correct an earlier suboptimal choice of path. Without that reverse residual capacity, flow sent along (u, v) could never be reduced, and the algorithm could get stuck short of the true maximum.

cards.prompt: ___ repeatedly finds an augmenting path, pushes flow equal to its residual capacity along it, and repeats until none remains. It leaves the choice of *which* augmenting path unspecified, and that choice matters: with a poor choice, its running time can be as bad as O(E * |f*|), where |f*| is the value of the maximum flow, since integer capacities can force one unit of flow to be added per iteration in the worst case.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)

cards.prompt: What specifically makes generic Ford-Fulkerson's running time pseudo-polynomial (depending on the numeric value of the max flow, not just V and E)?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)

choices.text: An arbitrary choice of augmenting path can force each iteration to increase the flow by as little as one unit, so the number of iterations can equal the max flow's numeric value
It always uses a depth-first search, which is asymptotically slow
The residual network can have more edges than the original graph
It cannot handle networks with integer capacities

cards.prompt: ___ is Ford-Fulkerson with one specific choice: always pick the shortest augmenting path in the residual network, measured by number of edges, found by running BFS from s. That choice alone bounds the number of iterations by O(VE), giving a total running time of O(V E^2).
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)

cards.prompt: What specific rule does Edmonds-Karp add to generic Ford-Fulkerson, and what running time does that rule guarantee?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)
cards.answer: It always chooses the shortest augmenting path (fewest edges) via BFS on the residual network, which bounds the algorithm to O(VE) iterations and O(VE^2) total running time — independent of the numeric flow value.

cards.prompt: Explain what a cut of a flow network is, and why the value of any flow is bounded above by the capacity of every cut — the fact that underlies the max-flow min-cut theorem.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)

cards.prompt: The ___ ties the whole algorithm to a duality result: the value of a maximum flow equals the capacity of a minimum cut, and Ford-Fulkerson terminates exactly when no augmenting path exists — which happens precisely when the current flow saturates some cut, certifying that flow as maximum.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 24 (Maximum Flow)

cards.prompt: A ___ of a graph is any partition of V into two disjoint sets S and V - S. An edge crosses the cut if it has one endpoint in each set. The cut property states: for any cut (S, V - S), if an edge (u, v) is a minimum-weight edge crossing that cut, then (u, v) is a safe edge for some MST — i.e., there exists an MST that contains it.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: A cut of a graph is any partition of V into two disjoint sets S and V - S. An edge crosses the cut if it has one endpoint in each set. The ___ states: for any cut (S, V - S), if an edge (u, v) is a minimum-weight edge crossing that cut, then (u, v) is a safe edge for some MST — i.e., there exists an MST that contains it.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: An edge is ___ for a set A of edges (already known to be a subset of some MST) if A union {(u, v)} is also a subset of some MST. The generic algorithm just repeatedly adds safe edges until it has a spanning tree — the whole design problem is finding safe edges cheaply.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: Why does the cut property guarantee that a minimum-weight edge crossing a cut is safe, given some edge set A already known to lie in an MST?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)
cards.answer: Take any MST T that contains A but not this minimum-weight crossing edge (u, v); T must contain some other edge crossing the same cut to stay connected. Swapping that other edge out for (u, v) cannot increase the total weight, since (u, v) is minimum-weight across the cut, and the result is still a spanning tree containing A union {(u, v)} — so an MST containing A union {(u, v)} exists.

cards.prompt: Which cut should you choose for a given set A of edges known to be safe, when applying the cut property to find the next safe edge?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

choices.text: Any cut that respects A — one where no edge of A crosses it
The cut with the fewest crossing edges
The cut separating the highest-weight vertex from the rest
There is no restriction; any cut works for any A

cards.prompt: A cut ___ A if no edge in A crosses it. The theorem's guarantee only holds for a light edge across a cut that respects the current A — choosing a cut that some edge of A crosses would let the property recommend an edge that creates a cycle with A.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: What condition must a cut satisfy for the cut property to correctly identify a safe edge to add to the current edge set A?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)
cards.answer: The cut must respect A — no edge already in A may cross it — and the edge chosen must be a minimum-weight edge crossing that cut.

cards.prompt: Explain why the generic MST algorithm's correctness proof, built on the cut property, works regardless of which specific safe edge is chosen at each step — what does that imply about the two concrete algorithms (Kruskal's and Prim's) that instantiate this generic scheme with different edge-choice strategies?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: The MST problem also relies on the graph being ___; if it is not, no spanning tree exists at all, and the generic algorithm's loop condition (adding edges until a spanning tree forms) never terminates.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 21 (Minimum Spanning Trees)

cards.prompt: ___ of edge (u, v) tests whether going through u improves the current best known distance to v — if d[u] + w(u, v) < d[v], it sets d[v] = d[u] + w(u, v) and pi[v] = u. No shortest-path algorithm in this category does anything structurally different from repeated relaxation — they differ only in which edges they relax, and in what order.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Correctness rests on the ___ property of shortest paths: any subpath of a shortest path is itself a shortest path between its own endpoints. This is what lets relaxation build a shortest path incrementally from shortest sub-paths, rather than needing to consider whole paths at once.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Why does the optimal-substructure property justify building a shortest path via repeated relaxation of individual edges, rather than examining whole candidate paths?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)
cards.answer: Because every subpath of a shortest path is itself shortest between its endpoints, a shortest path to v that passes through u must have, as its prefix, a shortest path to u — so once d[u] holds the true shortest distance, testing the single edge (u, v) via relaxation is enough to correctly extend that optimal prefix, with no need to reconsider the path built so far.

cards.prompt: ___ handles graphs with negative-weight edges — something Dijkstra's algorithm cannot do correctly. It works by relaxing every edge in the graph, in an arbitrary fixed order, for |V| - 1 rounds, then checking every edge once more for a possible further improvement.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Bellman-Ford handles graphs with negative-weight edges — something Dijkstra's algorithm cannot do correctly. It works by relaxing every edge in the graph, in an arbitrary fixed order, for ___ rounds, then checking every edge once more for a possible further improvement.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: Why does Bellman-Ford relax every edge exactly |V| - 1 times?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

choices.text: Any shortest path visits at most |V| - 1 edges, so |V| - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge suffice to propagate the correct distance along the longest possible shortest path
It matches the number of edges in a sparse graph
It is the number of rounds needed for a priority queue to empty
It bounds the number of negative edges the graph can contain

cards.prompt: Bellman-Ford detects a ___ reachable from the source with one extra pass after the main loop: if any edge can still be relaxed — its endpoints' distances would still strictly improve — some cycle on that edge's path must have negative total weight, since otherwise |V| - 1 rounds would already have converged.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: What does it mean, and what does it imply, if some edge (u, v) can still be relaxed after Bellman-Ford's |V| - 1 main rounds have completed?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)
cards.answer: It means d[v] > d[u] + w(u, v) still holds; since |V| - 1 rounds already suffice to find every true shortest-path distance in a graph with no negative-weight cycle reachable from s, this can only happen if a negative-weight cycle reachable from s exists, in which case shortest-path distances are undefined (unbounded below).

cards.prompt: Explain why a negative-weight cycle makes "shortest path" an undefined concept for any vertex reachable from it, rather than merely a very small number.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 22 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

cards.prompt: The first pass runs plain DFS on G and records each vertex's finish time. The second pass runs DFS again, but on the ___ (every edge direction reversed) — and critically, it considers vertices as roots in decreasing order of the finish times from the first pass. Each resulting depth-first tree is exactly one SCC.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Why does running the second DFS on the transpose graph, rather than on G again, matter for the correctness of this algorithm?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: Running DFS again on G would let a tree grow across SCC boundaries whenever one SCC has an edge into another, since that edge is still followable forward. Reversing to G^T removes exactly the edges that would let a tree escape "downstream" into a different SCC that the current one can reach but that cannot reach back, while preserving reachability within each SCC (since SCC membership itself is symmetric).

cards.prompt: In the second DFS pass (on G^T), why must vertices be tried as roots in decreasing order of first-pass finish time?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

choices.text: It guarantees each new root starts a component whose SCC has no as-yet-unvisited SCC reachable from it in G^T, so the resulting tree cannot spill past its own SCC's boundary
It makes the second DFS run faster asymptotically
It ensures the transpose graph is explored in the same order as G
It guarantees every resulting tree is a single vertex

cards.prompt: What does each tree in the depth-first forest produced by the second DFS pass (on G^T, in decreasing finish-time order) correspond to?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: Exactly one strongly connected component of the original graph G.

cards.prompt: The key structural fact that makes the whole scheme work is about the component graph: contracting each SCC of G to a single vertex always yields a ___ — there can be no cycle among SCCs, since any cycle spanning multiple SCCs would merge them into one larger SCC by definition. Decreasing finish-time order effectively processes SCCs in a topological order of that component DAG, source SCCs first.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Explain, in terms of the component graph being a DAG, why picking the next DFS root in G^T by decreasing first-pass finish time always picks a vertex from an SCC that has no edge, in G^T, leading out to an as-yet-unvisited SCC — and why that is exactly what keeps each second-pass tree confined to one SCC.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Because it is two DFS passes plus building the transpose, the total running time is ___, the same asymptotic bound as a single DFS.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: A ___ (directed acyclic graph) is exactly a directed graph with no cycle, and topological sort is defined only for DAGs — a cyclic dependency graph has no valid ordering, since some task would need to precede itself.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: TOPOLOGICAL-SORT runs DFS on the graph and, as each vertex finishes, inserts it onto the front of a linked list; the final list, read front to back, is the topological order. Equivalently: sort vertices by ___.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Why does ordering vertices by decreasing DFS finish time produce a valid topological order?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: For any edge (u, v) in a DAG, u must finish after v — if DFS discovers u first, v cannot be a white-path ancestor of u without creating a cycle, and if v is discovered first it must finish before u's DFS-VISIT returns (since a DAG has no back edge from u to an already-gray v). Either way f[u] > f[v], so decreasing-finish-time order always lists u before v.

cards.prompt: Why must the graph be acyclic for a topological sort to exist at all?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

choices.text: A cycle forces some vertex to both precede and follow another, which no linear order can satisfy
DFS cannot compute finish times on a cyclic graph
Cyclic graphs are always disconnected
A cycle makes the graph's adjacency list infinite

cards.prompt: The correctness argument rests on one fact about DFS on a DAG: it never produces a ___. A back edge (u, v) means v is an ancestor of u still on the recursion stack when u is discovered — but that implies a path v -> ... -> u plus the edge u -> v, which is a cycle. So a DAG's absence of cycles is equivalent to its DFS producing no back edges.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: What kind of edge does a DFS of a directed graph produce if and only if the graph contains a cycle?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)
cards.answer: A back edge — an edge from a vertex to one of its own ancestors in the depth-first forest, still gray (on the stack) at the time it's encountered.

cards.prompt: Explain how you would use a single DFS traversal to detect whether a directed graph is a DAG, without running a separate topological sort afterward — what exact condition, checked during the traversal, tells you a cycle exists?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: Because it is built on DFS, topological sort runs in ___: Theta(V + E) for the DFS itself, plus Theta(V) to prepend each finished vertex, which does not change the asymptotic total.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 20 (Elementary Graph Algorithms)

cards.prompt: The first fork is ___: heapsort and quicksort work on any totally ordered type using only a `<=` operator and are bound by Omega(n lg n) (see this category's lower-bound note); counting sort, radix sort, and bucket sort need structured keys — a bounded integer range, digits, or a known distribution — but can reach linear time in exchange.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6-8

cards.prompt: What single property must the elements have for a comparison sort to work as a general-purpose sort on arbitrary data, independent of any assumption about key structure or distribution?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6-8
cards.answer: A total order — a working `<=` or three-way comparison — on the elements; this is exactly what makes comparison sorts like heapsort and quicksort universally applicable, at the cost of the Omega(n lg n) lower bound that comes with relying only on comparisons.

cards.prompt: Stability — preserving equal keys' relative order — splits the category along different lines than the comparison/non-comparison one. Counting sort and (LSD) radix sort are stable by construction, as this category's counting-sort note details; heapsort and Lomuto quicksort are ___, since both rely on swaps that can reorder equal keys.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6-8

cards.prompt: Which pairing of algorithm and stability is correct?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6-8

choices.text: Counting sort is stable; heapsort is not
Heapsort is stable; counting sort is not
Both heapsort and counting sort are stable
Neither heapsort nor counting sort is stable

cards.prompt: Why can quicksort in practice often outperform heapsort despite both being O(n lg n)-class algorithms (quicksort's average case), even though heapsort has the better worst-case guarantee?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6-8
cards.answer: Quicksort's partitioning touches memory in mostly sequential, cache-friendly scans and its inner loop is simpler, while heapsort's array-as-tree access pattern jumps between indices that are far apart, causing more cache misses per comparison — so quicksort's practical constant factor is usually smaller despite its Theta(n^2) worst case (mitigated by randomization, per this category's randomized-quicksort note).

cards.prompt: Explain why a hybrid like introsort needs *both* a fast average-case algorithm and a worst-case-safe fallback, rather than just always using the worst-case-safe one — what does the fallback cost when it is never triggered, and what does skipping it cost when it is needed?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6-8

cards.prompt: Heapsort, quicksort, and merge sort all reach Theta(n lg n) worst-case or expected time, and none of them beats it. This note explains why: any algorithm that decides the output order only by comparing pairs of elements — a ___ — cannot do better than that bound, no matter how cleverly it chooses which pairs to compare.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: The argument models any comparison sort as a ___: an internal node is one comparison, its two children are the two possible outcomes, and a leaf is a fully determined output permutation. A path from root to leaf is one execution of the algorithm on some input.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: Why must a correct comparison-sort decision tree have at least n! leaves?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: Every one of the n! possible orderings of n distinct elements is a permutation the algorithm must be able to output on some input, and each leaf can correspond to at most one output permutation, so a tree with fewer than n! leaves would leave some permutation unreachable — meaning the algorithm would sort at least one input wrong.

cards.prompt: What does Stirling's approximation let us conclude about lg(n!), and what bound on comparisons does that give?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: lg(n!) is Omega(n lg n), so any comparison-sort decision tree has height Omega(n lg n) — and since the tree's height is exactly the worst-case number of comparisons on some input, every comparison sort makes Omega(n lg n) comparisons in the worst case.

cards.prompt: The decision-tree argument bounds which quantity?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

choices.text: The worst-case number of element-to-element comparisons any comparison sort must make
The average-case running time of quicksort specifically
The best-case running time of insertion sort
The number of swaps any in-place sort must make

cards.prompt: Because heapsort and merge sort both achieve O(n lg n) worst case, and the lower bound says Omega(n lg n) is unavoidable for this whole class, they are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts: ___ is the best any comparison sort can guarantee.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: Precisely what class of algorithms does this bound constrain?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: Only algorithms that determine relative order exclusively through pairwise comparisons of elements — it says nothing about algorithms that instead use elements' actual values, such as counting sort or radix sort, which sidestep the bound entirely by never building a comparison-based decision tree.

cards.prompt: Explain why counting sort running in O(n + k) time does not contradict the Omega(n lg n) comparison-sort lower bound — what assumption of the decision-tree argument does it violate?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: Why does the final placement loop iterate over A from right to left rather than left to right?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: Processing back to front places equal keys into the output in the same relative order they had in the input, because the last-seen copy of a repeated key claims the highest remaining slot in C first and earlier copies claim progressively lower slots — reversing the scan direction would still sort correctly but would reverse the relative order of equal keys.

cards.prompt: An algorithm is ___ if elements with equal keys keep their original relative order in the output. Counting sort achieves this only because of the specific right-to-left placement above — it is not an automatic property of "sorting by counting."
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: Why does stability matter for a sort used as a subroutine, even when the final keys being compared are all distinct?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: A stable sort lets you sort records by one key while preserving whatever order a previous sort established on a different key — for example sorting by last name, then stably by first name, keeps same-first-name groups sorted by last name; radix sort depends on exactly this property, since it repeatedly re-sorts the whole array by one digit at a time.

cards.prompt: Counting sort's O(n + k) running time depends critically on which assumption?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

choices.text: Keys are integers in a known range 0..k
The input is already nearly sorted
Keys are drawn from a continuous, uniformly distributed range
The array is small enough to fit in cache

cards.prompt: What happens to counting sort's running time guarantee when the key range k is much larger than n, and why?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: The bound O(n + k) is dominated by the k term, so it stops being linear in the input size and can become far worse than any Theta(n lg n) comparison sort — the algorithm needs the range to be O(n) (or close to it) for its linear-time advantage to actually hold.

cards.prompt: Explain why counting sort's O(n + k) bound is not a violation of the comparison-sort lower bound, connecting it back to what a decision tree assumes about how the algorithm accesses keys.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: A max-heap satisfies the ___: every node's key is greater than or equal to both of its children's keys. This says nothing about left-versus-right ordering, only parent-versus-child, so a heap is much weaker — and cheaper to maintain — than a fully sorted array.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6 (Heapsort)

cards.prompt: On a subtree of height `h`, one call does O(1) work plus a recursive call into a subtree of height `h-1`, giving MAX-HEAPIFY a worst-case running time of ___, proportional to the heap's height.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6 (Heapsort)

cards.prompt: Why is BUILD-MAX-HEAP's running time O(n) rather than the O(n lg n) suggested by the per-call bound?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6 (Heapsort)
cards.answer: Summing each node's actual work by height rather than using a uniform O(lg n) bound gives n * sum over h of h / 2^(h+1), and that series converges to a constant, so the total is O(n) — the O(n lg n) figure only holds if every node were charged for a full sift down to the leaves, which almost none of them do.

cards.prompt: Given BUILD-MAX-HEAP is O(n), what does heapsort's overall running time work out to?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6 (Heapsort)
cards.answer: Building the heap is O(n), and then n-1 iterations each swap the max to the end and call MAX-HEAPIFY (O(lg n)) on the shrunken heap, giving O(n) + O(n lg n), which is O(n lg n) overall.

cards.prompt: Which statement about BUILD-MAX-HEAP's asymptotic running time is correct?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6 (Heapsort)

choices.text: It is Theta(n), tighter than the O(n lg n) bound a naive per-call analysis suggests
It is Theta(n lg n), matching heapsort's overall bound
It is Theta(n^2) because every node may sift all the way to a leaf
It depends on whether the input is already sorted

cards.prompt: Heapsort itself repeats two steps n-1 times: swap the root (the maximum, by the heap property) with the last element of the heap, shrink the heap's logical size by one, and call MAX-HEAPIFY on the new root. It runs in-place and needs no extra array, but it is ___, since swaps can reorder equal keys arbitrarily.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6 (Heapsort)

cards.prompt: Explain why a heap makes a good priority queue but a poor structure for finding an arbitrary element quickly — connect this to what the heap property does and does not constrain.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 6 (Heapsort)

cards.prompt: Why does recursing into only one side, rather than both, change the running time compared to randomized quicksort?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 9 (Medians and Order Statistics)
cards.answer: Quicksort's Theta(n lg n) comes from work being repeated at every level across both halves; select only ever recurses into one subarray per call, so the geometric shrinkage of typical partition sizes makes the total work across all levels sum to a constant factor of the first level's n, rather than growing with recursion depth.

cards.prompt: RANDOMIZED-SELECT runs in ___ O(n) time, over the algorithm's own random pivot choices — exactly like randomized quicksort, its worst case is still Theta(n^2), reached when every random pivot happens to produce a maximally unbalanced split.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 9 (Medians and Order Statistics)

cards.prompt: RANDOMIZED-SELECT's O(n) running time bound is best described as which of these?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 9 (Medians and Order Statistics)

choices.text: Expected time, averaged over the algorithm's random pivot choices; a Theta(n^2) worst case still exists
Worst-case time, guaranteed on every input and every run
Amortized time over a sequence of calls
Best-case time only, degrading to Theta(n lg n) on average

cards.prompt: CLRS's other selection algorithm, often called `SELECT` or the "median-of-medians" algorithm, replaces the random pivot with a deliberately constructed good one: it divides the array into groups of 5, finds each group's median (by brute-force sorting of just 5 elements), recursively finds the ___, and uses that as the pivot.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 9 (Medians and Order Statistics)

cards.prompt: Why does using the median of medians as the pivot guarantee a good split, unlike an arbitrary deterministic choice such as "always the last element"?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 9 (Medians and Order Statistics)
cards.answer: The median of medians is provably greater than at least half of the group medians and less than the other half, and each of those group medians is itself the middle of 5 elements, which forces the chosen pivot to be larger than roughly 3/10 of all elements and smaller than roughly 3/10 of all elements regardless of the input's arrangement — guaranteeing a split that is bounded away from 0-to-(n-1) no matter what the adversary supplies.

cards.prompt: Median-of-medians SELECT achieves ___ O(n) time — this is the key contrast with RANDOMIZED-SELECT: no input and no adversary can push it past linear time, at the cost of a larger constant factor and a more involved recursive structure (it recurses both to find the median of medians and to search the correctly-sized remaining side).
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 9 (Medians and Order Statistics)

cards.prompt: State precisely which of RANDOMIZED-SELECT and median-of-medians SELECT gives an expected linear-time guarantee and which gives a worst-case linear-time guarantee, and explain in one sentence each why that specific guarantee holds.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 9 (Medians and Order Statistics)

cards.prompt: `LOMUTO-PARTITION(A, p, r)` fixes `A[r]` as the ___ and walks an index `i` through `A[p..r-1]`, tracking the boundary of elements known to be `<= pivot`. Whenever the current element is `<= pivot`, it advances that boundary and swaps the element into it; at the end it swaps the pivot itself into place just past the boundary.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

cards.prompt: Why does Lomuto partitioning make only one pass over the subarray?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)
cards.answer: It maintains a single invariant as it scans left to right — everything at or before index `i` is `<= pivot` and everything between `i+1` and the scan pointer `j` is `> pivot` — so one swap per "small" element found is enough to keep both regions correct without a second pass.

cards.prompt: What is the asymptotic running time of a single call to LOMUTO-PARTITION on a subarray of length n?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)
cards.answer: Theta(n), since it does exactly one constant-time comparison (and at most one swap) per element in a single left-to-right scan.

cards.prompt: Quicksort's recursion structure means its running time depends entirely on how evenly each partition splits the subarray. A split into two equal halves recurses like merge sort's, giving a recursion tree of depth ___ and O(n lg n) total work.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

cards.prompt: Which specific input triggers Lomuto quicksort's worst case, and what recursion does it produce?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)
cards.answer: An already-sorted (or reverse-sorted) array, when the pivot is always chosen as the last element: the partition then puts every other element on one side and none on the other, so each call recurses on a subarray of length n-1, producing a completely unbalanced recursion of depth n and Theta(n^2) total work.

cards.prompt: Deterministically picking the last element as pivot, what is quicksort's worst-case running time on an input that is already sorted?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

choices.text: Theta(n^2)
Theta(n lg n)
Theta(n)
Theta(lg n)

cards.prompt: Explain why an unbalanced 1-to-(n-1) split at every level of the recursion, rather than an unbalanced-but-still-fractional split like 1-to-9, is what actually produces the Theta(n^2) worst case — what changes about the recursion tree's depth and per-level work.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

cards.prompt: LSD radix sort sorts multi-digit keys by repeatedly sorting on a single digit, starting from the ___ digit and working toward the most significant, using a stable sort as the subroutine at each pass.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: Why must the per-digit subroutine be stable for radix sort to work at all?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: Each pass only distinguishes elements by one digit, so elements that tie on that digit must keep the relative order established by all the previous (less significant) passes; an unstable subroutine would scramble that accumulated ordering, and the final result would not be correctly sorted on the digits already processed.

cards.prompt: With `d` digits, each in the range `0` to `k`, and each counting-sort pass costing `Theta(n + k)`, radix sort's total running time is `Theta(d(n + k))`. Choosing a digit size so `k = Theta(n)` makes each pass ___, so the whole sort is `Theta(d*n)` — linear in `n` for any fixed number of digits `d`.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: Why does radix sort require a stable sort as its per-digit subroutine, specifically?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

choices.text: So ties on the current digit preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits processed in earlier passes
So the algorithm can run in-place without extra memory
So the algorithm works correctly on keys of unequal length
So each pass can run in parallel with the others

cards.prompt: Bucket sort takes a different assumption: it works well when input keys are ___ over a known range, typically real numbers in `[0, 1)`. It divides the range into `n` equal-sized buckets, scatters each input element into its bucket in O(1), sorts each bucket (commonly with insertion sort, since buckets are expected to be small), then concatenates the buckets in order.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: What specific assumption about the input does bucket sort's expected O(n) analysis rely on, and what happens to that bound if the assumption fails?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)
cards.answer: It relies on keys being drawn independently from a uniform distribution over the range, so that each bucket receives O(1) elements on average; if the input is skewed so most keys land in one bucket, that bucket's insertion sort degrades toward its own worst case, and the overall running time can rise toward Theta(n^2) even though the algorithm never compares keys across buckets.

cards.prompt: Contrast what "linear time" costs each of counting sort, radix sort, and bucket sort in terms of the assumption it makes about the input — radix sort's assumption is about key structure, and bucket sort's is about a probability distribution, not a fixed range. Explain why neither assumption is needed by a comparison sort, and why that is exactly the tradeoff for beating Omega(n lg n).
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 8 (Sorting in Linear Time)

cards.prompt: The previous note showed deterministic Lomuto quicksort has a Theta(n^2) worst case on inputs an adversary can construct in advance, such as an already-sorted array. `RANDOMIZED-PARTITION` fixes the *attacker's* leverage, not the worst case itself, by swapping `A[r]` with a ___ element of `A[p..r]` before calling ordinary Lomuto partitioning on it.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

cards.prompt: What is the key property CLRS exploits about when two elements get compared in quicksort?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)
cards.answer: Two elements are compared at most once in the entire run, and only if one of them is chosen as a pivot before any element with a rank strictly between them is — so the total comparison count over the run is exactly the sum of these Theta(n^2) pairwise indicator variables.

cards.prompt: Randomized quicksort's expected running time on any input, worst case included, is ___. This holds for every input array, including the ones that force Theta(n^2) on the deterministic version, because the expectation is taken over the algorithm's own random pivot choices, not over some assumed distribution of inputs.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

cards.prompt: Which best describes the source of the randomness in randomized quicksort's O(n lg n) expected-time bound?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

choices.text: The algorithm's own random pivot choices, averaged over all its possible runs on one fixed input
An assumption that the input array itself is drawn uniformly at random
The random assignment of elements to processors
Randomized rounding of the comparison results

cards.prompt: Is there still an input, or a sequence of coin flips, that makes randomized quicksort take Theta(n^2) time?
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)
cards.answer: Yes — for any fixed sequence of random choices there exists some input that produces an unbalanced Theta(n^2) split at every level, so the Theta(n^2) worst case still exists in the sample space; what changes is that no adversary who only sees the input in advance (and not the random bits) can *force* that run, because the same input yields a fast run under almost all other random choices.

cards.prompt: Explain precisely why "expected O(n lg n) running time" and "worst-case O(n lg n) running time" are different claims, and which one randomized quicksort actually achieves.
citations: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms 4e, Ch. 7 (Quicksort)

cards.prompt: A database is serializable but not linearizable. What can still go wrong?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

choices.text: A client can read stale data from a replica even though it was written moments ago by another client, because serializability doesn't constrain recency
Transactions can leave the database in an inconsistent state
Two transactions can both read and write the same row without any isolation
The database can lose committed data on a crash

cards.prompt: Linearizability is a ___ guarantee on single objects; serializability is an isolation guarantee across transactions.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

cards.prompt: Linearizability is a recency guarantee on single objects; serializability is an ___ guarantee across transactions.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

cards.prompt: What does the P in CAP actually mean, and why is "pick two of three" a misleading framing?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9
cards.answer: Network partitions are not a choice but a fact about deploying over an unreliable network — they will happen. The real decision a system designer faces is how the system behaves when a partition occurs: either remain available and risk returning inconsistent (stale or conflicting) data, or refuse to serve some requests to preserve consistency. "Pick two of three" wrongly implies you can choose to avoid P, when in fact CA (consistent and available) is only achievable in the absence of any partition at all.

cards.prompt: Which statement about CAP is accurate?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

choices.text: During a network partition, a system must choose between remaining available (possibly inconsistent) or consistent (possibly unavailable); it cannot choose to avoid partitions
A well-engineered system can be simultaneously consistent, available, and partition-tolerant at all times
CAP proves that all distributed databases are equally unreliable
Partition tolerance is an optional feature that most production systems disable

cards.prompt: Total order broadcast is a protocol guaranteeing that messages are delivered to every node in the ___, reliably (no message is lost) — it is equivalent in difficulty to solving consensus, and can be used to implement single-leader replication's operation log or to build a linearizable storage service.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

cards.prompt: Why is implementing linearizable compare-and-set storage considered equivalent in difficulty to solving consensus?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

choices.text: Both require all nodes to agree on a single, totally ordered sequence of operations despite failures and network delays — solving one lets you build the other
Linearizability requires no coordination between nodes at all
Consensus algorithms cannot tolerate any node failures, unlike linearizable storage
Compare-and-set operations do not require ordering, only atomicity

cards.prompt: Consensus algorithms (e.g. Raft, Paxos) must satisfy uniform agreement (no two nodes decide differently), integrity (no node decides twice), validity (a decided value was actually proposed by some node), and ___ (every node that doesn't crash eventually decides some value) — this last property is why consensus is provably impossible to guarantee in a fully asynchronous system with even one faulty node (the FLP result), which is why practical algorithms rely on timeouts and partial synchrony assumptions.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

cards.prompt: Two nodes in a leaderless quorum system use w + r > n for reads and writes. Explain a scenario where this inequality still fails to return the most recent write, despite being satisfied.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 9

cards.prompt: Which situation favors a document model over a normalized relational schema?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 2

choices.text: Data with a tree-like structure that is almost always loaded and updated as one self-contained unit
Data with many-to-many relationships requiring frequent joins across entities
Data requiring multi-object transactions spanning many collections
Data whose schema must be enforced strictly at write time

cards.prompt: Document databases are typically described as ___, meaning the structure of the data is implicit and only interpreted when the application reads it; a relational database with a fixed schema is schema-on-write, meaning the database enforces structure at write time.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 2

cards.prompt: Explain why schema-on-read is often compared to dynamic typing in programming languages, and name one advantage this style has when an application's data structure changes frequently.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 2

cards.prompt: Vertices in a ___ can have arbitrary key-value properties and one or more labels, and edges also carry a label describing the kind of relationship and can have their own properties.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 2

cards.prompt: Why are recursive many-hop relationship queries (e.g. "friends of friends of friends") typically awkward in a relational database but natural in a graph database?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 2

choices.text: SQL requires repeated joins or recursive CTEs for variable-depth traversal, while graph query languages traverse edges directly regardless of depth
Relational databases cannot store relationships between rows at all
Graph databases do not use disk-based storage, so traversal is always faster
SQL does not support the WHERE clause needed to filter friends

cards.prompt: What does "the network model" (a historical predecessor to relational databases) require that the relational model does not?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 2
cards.answer: The network model requires the application to navigate data by following explicit access paths (pointers between records) chosen in advance, whereas the relational model lets a query optimizer choose the access path automatically based on declarative queries.

cards.prompt: A client sends a write request and gets no response within its timeout. Why can't the client safely conclude the write did not happen?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 8

choices.text: The request, the processing, or the response could each have been delayed or lost independently — the write may have succeeded and only the acknowledgment was lost
TCP guarantees that a timeout always means the request was never received
Timeouts only occur when the server explicitly rejects a request
The client can always tell success from failure by checking its local clock

cards.prompt: Because failure detection via timeout can't distinguish a slow node from a dead one, choosing a timeout value is a tradeoff: too short and you declare healthy-but-slow nodes dead (spuriously triggering failover or duplicate work); too long and real failures take longer to detect, increasing the window of ___.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 8

cards.prompt: **Time-of-day clocks** (NTP-synchronized wall-clock time) can jump backward or forward and are unsuitable for measuring elapsed time or ordering events; ___ only ever move forward and are appropriate for measuring durations, but are meaningless to compare across different machines.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 8

cards.prompt: Why is it unsafe to use time-of-day clock timestamps from two different machines to determine which of two writes happened first?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 8

choices.text: Clocks on different machines drift and are only approximately synchronized, and a clock can even jump backward after NTP resync, so the timestamp order may not match the real causal order
Time-of-day clocks are not available on server hardware
Monotonic clocks must be used instead, and they are comparable across machines
Timestamps are always accurate to the nanosecond on modern hardware

cards.prompt: A ___ is a monotonically increasing number issued alongside a lock or lease grant; a resource being protected can then reject any write carrying a number lower than the highest one it has already seen, protecting against a paused process that wakes up believing it still holds the lock.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 8

cards.prompt: A client holds a lease on a storage service, then experiences a 30-second GC pause during which its lease expires and is granted to another client. Both clients then try to write. What prevents the stale client's write from corrupting data?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 8

choices.text: A fencing token: the storage service rejects the write carrying the older (lower) token, since a newer token has already been seen
The stale client's write is automatically delayed until its lease is valid again
TCP guarantees the stale client's connection is closed during the pause
The storage service trusts whichever write arrives first, regardless of token

cards.prompt: Why can't a distributed system simply ask "is this node still alive?" and get a reliable answer?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 8
cards.answer: Because the only way to ask is over the same asynchronous network that might be the thing failing — a lack of response is ambiguous between "the node is dead," "the node is just slow," and "the network dropped the request or response," so liveness can only ever be inferred via timeouts, never known for certain.

cards.prompt: Protocol Buffers and Thrift both encode fields using a numeric ___ (field number) instead of the field name, which keeps encoded messages compact since the schema (not the data) carries the field names.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4

cards.prompt: In Protocol Buffers, why must an existing field's tag number never be reused for a different field, even after the old field is removed?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4

choices.text: Old encoded data or old code still refers to that tag number, so reusing it would cause new code to misinterpret old data as the new field
Tag numbers are used to compute a checksum and must be globally unique across all schemas ever written
Protocol Buffers does not allow more than 100 tag numbers per message
Reusing a tag number would break the human-readable field names

cards.prompt: Avro takes a different approach from Protobuf/Thrift: it has no per-field tag numbers at all, and instead a reader decodes data using both the ___ and its own reader's schema, resolving differences between them field-by-field.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4

cards.prompt: Avro readers resolve schema differences by comparing the writer's schema to the reader's schema. What must accompany Avro-encoded data for this to work?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4

choices.text: Some way for the reader to obtain the exact schema the writer used (e.g. embedded, versioned in a registry, or negotiated per connection)
The reader's own schema must be sent alongside every record
Avro data is self-describing and requires no schema at all
A checksum of the data must match a checksum of the schema

cards.prompt: What problem do a "schema registry" and dataflow through a database (rather than only through service APIs) both illustrate about backward compatibility?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4
cards.answer: A value written once (to a database, or a message queue) may be read much later by code that didn't exist yet when it was written — so it is the newer code doing the reading of older data, the classic backward-compatibility direction, just stretched across an arbitrarily long time gap instead of a single rolling deployment window.

cards.prompt: Old (v1) code reads a record that was written by newer (v2) code, which added a field v1 has never seen. What must v1 do to stay forward compatible?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4

choices.text: Ignore the unknown field, but preserve it unchanged if it later rewrites the record, rather than silently dropping it
Reject the record because its schema doesn't match exactly
Automatically upgrade itself to understand the new field before proceeding
Convert the unknown field into a required field using a generated default

cards.prompt: Dataflow through services (REST/RPC) couples a request and response in time, but dataflow through a ___ decouples producers and consumers entirely — they don't call each other directly and don't even need to be running at the same time.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4

cards.prompt: A REST API adds a required (non-nullable, no default) new field to its JSON response. Explain which compatibility guarantee this breaks and for whom.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 4

cards.prompt: A table partitioned by key range uses an ever-increasing timestamp as its partition key. What problem does this cause?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 6

choices.text: All writes for "now" land on the same partition, creating a hot spot even though the cluster has many nodes
Range queries become impossible because timestamps cannot be compared
The database refuses to accept timestamp keys
Storage usage decreases because timestamps compress extremely well

cards.prompt: Hash partitioning distributes keys evenly but loses the ability to do efficient ___, because adjacent keys in the original key space no longer land on adjacent (or even nearby) partitions.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 6

cards.prompt: Why might a system deliberately use a compound key of (hashed portion, range portion) rather than hashing the entire key?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 6

choices.text: It spreads unrelated records across partitions while still allowing efficient range scans within one logical group, e.g. all of one user's records sorted by timestamp
It eliminates the need for replication
It guarantees perfectly equal partition sizes at all times
It removes the need for a partitioning scheme entirely

cards.prompt: Secondary indexes complicate partitioning because an indexed value usually doesn't align with the primary partitioning key. A ___ (local) index keeps each partition's index covering only its own documents, so a query on the secondary index must be sent to every partition (scatter/gather); a term-partitioned (global) index partitions the index itself by term, so a query can go to fewer partitions but writes may need to update partitions other than the one holding the document.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 6

cards.prompt: Explain why hashing a key modulo the number of nodes (`hash(key) % N`) is a poor rebalancing strategy when nodes are added or removed.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 6

cards.prompt: Request routing in a partitioned system needs a way for a client (or a load balancer) to know which node currently owns a given partition; this is commonly solved by an external coordination service (e.g. ZooKeeper) that tracks partition assignment and notifies routing tiers when it changes, keeping the assignment ___ consistent across the cluster.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 6

cards.prompt: Why do engineers report the p99 or p999 latency instead of the mean?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1

choices.text: The mean hides tail behavior that a meaningful fraction of users actually experience
The mean is mathematically impossible to compute for skewed data
Percentiles are always lower than the mean, so they look better in reports
Regulatory standards require percentile reporting for all APIs

cards.prompt: A fault is a component deviating from spec; a ___ is the system as a whole ceasing to provide the required service.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1

cards.prompt: Scalability is not a single number ("this system scales") but a question of how a system's performance responds as a specific ___ grows, such as requests per second, the ratio of reads to writes, or the number of simultaneously active users.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1

cards.prompt: What is the difference between scaling up and scaling out?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1
cards.answer: Scaling up (vertical) moves the workload to a more powerful single machine; scaling out (horizontal) distributes the workload across many smaller machines. Shared-nothing horizontal scaling is more common for very large workloads but introduces distributed-systems complexity that a single powerful machine avoids.

cards.prompt: A service that was fast with 10 requests/second becomes unusably slow at 10,000 requests/second even though the machine has spare CPU. Which load parameter most likely explains this?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1

choices.text: A parameter the original design didn't account for, e.g. fan-out per request or a shared lock's contention
The service is simply CPU-bound and needs a faster processor
HTTP itself cannot handle more than a few thousand requests per second
The percentile latency metric is being miscalculated

cards.prompt: Maintainability is often reduced to three overlapping goals: operability (making it easy for operations teams to keep the system running), simplicity (removing unnecessary complexity from the system so new engineers can understand it), and ___ (making it easy to adapt the system to new requirements as they inevitably arise).
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1

cards.prompt: A team says their system is "reliable" because it hasn't gone down in six months. Explain why this claim, on its own, says little about whether the system is actually fault-tolerant.
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1

cards.prompt: What is the main risk of allowing followers to serve reads in a single-leader system?
citations: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 5
