cards.prompt: A file descriptor returned by ___ is just a small integer index into a per-process table pointing at an open-file entry — it is not the file's contents, and two descriptors can point at independent positions within the same underlying file.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)

cards.prompt: Why doesn't write() guarantee data has reached disk when it returns?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: The OS typically buffers writes in memory (the page cache) and flushes them to disk later for performance, so a successful write() only guarantees the data is queued; fsync() (or similar) is needed to force it to durable storage before the call returns.

cards.prompt: A directory is not a special data structure at the file-system level — it is just a file whose contents are a list of ___ pairs, which is why directory operations (create, rename, list) are really just reads and writes of an ordinary file's data.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)

cards.prompt: What actually gets removed when unlink() is called on a file with one remaining hard link?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: Its directory entry is removed, and because the inode's link count then drops to zero, the inode and its data blocks are freed; if other hard links still point at the same inode, the data survives untouched.

cards.prompt: A file has two hard links, `a` and `b`, both pointing at the same inode. `a` is deleted. What happens to the file's data?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)

choices.text: It remains fully accessible through `b`, since the inode's link count is still above zero
It's deleted immediately, since deleting any link deletes the underlying data
It becomes read-only until `b` is also deleted
A private copy is silently made for `b`

cards.prompt: Why can a symbolic link "dangle" in a way a hard link cannot?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: A symlink stores a path string that is resolved fresh at access time, so if the target is deleted the symlink is left pointing at a name that no longer resolves; a hard link instead is another direct reference to the same inode, so it cannot outlive the data it names.

cards.prompt: Explain why a hard link and "the file it links to" are not actually distinguishable at the file-system level — why there is no original versus copy once both links exist.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)

cards.prompt: Flash memory can be read and written at ___ granularity but can only be erased at the larger block granularity (each such unit holds many pages), so overwriting even one of them in place would require first erasing — and therefore rewriting — the whole surrounding region.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

cards.prompt: Flash memory can be read and written at page granularity but can only be erased at the larger ___ granularity (each such unit holds many pages), so overwriting even one of them in place would require first erasing — and therefore rewriting — the whole surrounding region.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

cards.prompt: Why does an SSD write updates to a fresh page instead of overwriting in place?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: Overwriting in place would force erasing the whole containing block first, a comparatively slow operation, so instead the drive writes the new version to an already-erased page elsewhere and remaps the logical address to it, deferring the erase until garbage collection reclaims the old block later.

cards.prompt: The ___ maps the logical block addresses the OS uses to physical flash locations, hiding erase-before-write and block-level erase granularity from the file system entirely — to the OS, the SSD still looks like an ordinary block device.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

cards.prompt: Why does an SSD need internal garbage collection, like LFS's cleaner?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: The FTL's out-of-place writes leave old page versions behind as garbage inside blocks, just as LFS's segments do, so the FTL needs its own background process to reclaim blocks by copying any still-live pages forward before erasing them.

cards.prompt: Explain why wear levelling is necessary, given that each flash block can survive only a limited number of program/erase cycles before it becomes unreliable.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

cards.prompt: Without ___, an FTL that kept reusing the same handful of free blocks would wear those specific blocks out to failure long before the rest of the drive's capacity was ever touched, even though plenty of usable life remained elsewhere on the drive.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

cards.prompt: What does "write amplification" mean for an SSD?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: The ratio of physical flash writes actually performed to the logical writes the host requested; garbage collection copying live pages out of a block, plus erasing the whole block to reclaim only a fraction of dead pages in it, both add physical writes beyond what the host asked for.

cards.prompt: An OS issues one small logical write to an SSD. Why might the SSD perform noticeably more physical write and erase work than that single logical write implies?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

choices.text: Garbage collection may copy live pages out of the target block and erase the whole block before it can be reused, amplifying one logical write into several physical operations
SSDs always write every logical write to every block for redundancy
The FTL requires the OS to explicitly request a separate erase command for every write
Flash pages are always physically larger than the write, wasting the unused remainder

cards.prompt: A single disk access has three components: ___ (move the arm to the target track), rotational latency (wait for the target sector to spin under the head), and transfer time (actually read or write once positioned). Seek and rotation are pure overhead paid before any useful data moves.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)

cards.prompt: Why is sequential access on a disk far faster than random access to the same amount of data?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: Sequential access pays one seek and one rotational wait, then streams many contiguous sectors in a row; random access pays a fresh seek and rotational wait for nearly every block, and those mechanical delays dwarf the time actually spent transferring data.

cards.prompt: The ___ scheduler always services the pending request closest to the disk head's current position. It minimizes seek distance greedily, but a steady stream of nearby requests can keep pushing a distant request to the back indefinitely.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)

cards.prompt: How does the elevator (SCAN) algorithm avoid the starvation SSTF can cause?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: It sweeps the head in one direction, servicing every request in its path in position order, then reverses at the far end and sweeps back, so any single request's maximum wait is bounded by one sweep instead of being pushed back indefinitely by closer arrivals.

cards.prompt: Why might a disk report a write done before data reaches the platter?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: A disk with an on-board write-back cache can acknowledge a write as soon as it lands in that volatile buffer, trading a small window of vulnerability (power loss before the buffer flushes) for lower perceived write latency.

cards.prompt: A workload issues many small requests to scattered locations, arriving continuously. Compared with pure SSTF, what does SCAN most directly improve?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)

choices.text: Bounded worst-case wait for far-away requests, since the sweep must eventually reach them
Total seek distance, which SCAN always makes smaller than SSTF
Rotational latency, which SCAN eliminates entirely
Transfer time per request, which SCAN halves on average

cards.prompt: Explain why disk scheduling can change total service time even though the same requests eventually get serviced and the same data is read or written either way.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)

cards.prompt: The simplest way to drive a device is ___: repeatedly read the status register in a loop until it reports the device is ready. That's simple but wastes CPU cycles spinning while a slow device does its work.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)

cards.prompt: Why do fast devices sometimes perform better with polling than with interrupts?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: An interrupt costs a context switch and trap-handling overhead; if a device usually finishes before that overhead would even be paid, briefly polling is cheaper than triggering, delivering, and dispatching an interrupt for a result that was already ready by the time it arrived.

cards.prompt: On completion, a slower device instead raises ___, a hardware signal that traps the CPU into a pre-registered handler, letting the CPU run other work while waiting rather than spinning on a status register.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)

cards.prompt: Why do high-throughput devices batch interrupts instead of firing one each?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: Interrupt handling carries a fixed per-interrupt cost (trap, register save, handler dispatch), so coalescing many completed operations into one interrupt amortizes that fixed cost across all of them, at the price of delaying notification for whichever operation finished first.

cards.prompt: Without ___, the CPU itself must copy every byte of a large transfer between a device and memory through the data register, one word at a time — wasteful for anything beyond a few bytes.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)

cards.prompt: What does a DMA controller let the CPU skip during a large data transfer?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: The OS hands the DMA controller a source, destination, and length, and the controller moves the data between device and memory on its own, interrupting the CPU only once when the whole transfer completes rather than once per word copied.

cards.prompt: A disk request takes 5ms to complete, and handling an interrupt costs about 2 microseconds of overhead. Which approach best uses the CPU while waiting?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)

choices.text: Interrupt-driven waiting, so the CPU can run other work during the 5ms
Busy-wait polling, since 5ms is a short amount of time
DMA instead of interrupts, since DMA replaces interrupt-driven waiting entirely
Disabling the device driver until the device signals readiness on its own

cards.prompt: Explain why polling and interrupts are not mutually exclusive strategies, and why a driver might deliberately poll for a short window before arming an interrupt instead of committing to one approach.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)

cards.prompt: LFS buffers writes in memory and flushes them together as one large ___ write, turning many small, scattered updates into a single efficient streaming write to the next free region of disk.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)

cards.prompt: Why can't LFS simply update an inode in place, the way FFS does?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: Updating in place would mean seeking back to that inode's old, fixed disk location on every write, reintroducing exactly the random-access cost LFS exists to avoid; instead LFS writes the updated inode to whatever the next free spot in the current write happens to be.

cards.prompt: Because inodes move on every update, LFS adds an ___ translating inode numbers to their current on-disk location — itself written to the log rather than kept at one fixed spot.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)

cards.prompt: Why must even the imap itself avoid a single fixed disk location?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: A fixed imap location would need an in-place update on every write, the exact random-access cost LFS was built to eliminate; so LFS logs imap updates too, and keeps only a small, fixed checkpoint region to bootstrap finding the current imap after a restart.

cards.prompt: Explain why old versions of overwritten blocks are left behind as "dead" data in earlier parts of the log, rather than being erased immediately at the moment a newer version is written.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)

cards.prompt: A background ___ process identifies segments holding mostly dead blocks, copies their few remaining live blocks forward into a fresh segment, and frees the old segment for reuse.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)

cards.prompt: Why does cleaning cost more as a segment's fraction of live data increases?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: A mostly-dead segment yields a lot of reclaimed space for very little copying, but a mostly-live segment forces the cleaner to read and rewrite almost as much data as it frees, so cleaning nearly-full segments has poor amortized efficiency compared to cleaning mostly-empty ones.

cards.prompt: LFS just finished writing several updated blocks. Where does it place a data block belonging to a file whose inode lives at a completely different disk location?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)

choices.text: Wherever the current write's next free slot is — LFS never seeks back to a fixed home location for an update
At the exact same offset the block held before, overwriting it in place
In a fixed region reserved per file, adjacent to nothing else
Immediately next to the inode, regardless of where the current log write is

cards.prompt: ___ stripes data across disks with no redundancy at all: it gains capacity and parallel performance, but tolerates zero disk failures — losing any one drive loses data, since no other disk holds a copy or a way to reconstruct it.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)

cards.prompt: Why does RAID-1 (mirroring) cost the most usable capacity among common RAID levels?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: Every block is written twice, to two separate disks, so exactly half of the raw capacity across the array is ever usable no matter how many mirrored pairs are added.

cards.prompt: ___ dedicates one disk entirely to parity, computed across the corresponding blocks on the other disks. Because every write must also update that one parity disk, it becomes a bottleneck whenever writes happen concurrently, even though the data disks themselves could be written in parallel.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)

cards.prompt: How does RAID-5 fix RAID-4's parity-disk bottleneck without adding disks?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: RAID-5 rotates which physical disk holds parity from one stripe to the next instead of dedicating a single disk to it, so parity writes are spread across every drive and no one disk absorbs the write load of the whole array.

cards.prompt: RAID-5 tolerates exactly ___ disk failure per stripe: losing a second disk before the array finishes rebuilding from the first loses data, because a stripe's parity can only reconstruct a single missing block, not two.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)

cards.prompt: What does RAID-6 add over RAID-5, and what does that buy?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: A second, independently computed parity block per stripe, so the array can reconstruct data even when any two disks fail at the same time, not just one.

cards.prompt: A RAID-5 array has one failed disk and is mid-rebuild when a second disk fails before the rebuild finishes. What happens?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)

choices.text: Data is lost — RAID-5's single parity block can only recover from one failure per stripe
The array keeps running normally using the remaining parity
RAID-5 automatically reconfigures itself into RAID-6 to absorb the second failure
Only the blocks written during the rebuild window are lost; the rest survive

cards.prompt: Explain the "small write problem" in parity-based RAID (RAID-4 and RAID-5): why updating a single data block requires more disk I/O than simply writing that one block would on its own.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)

cards.prompt: Why can't the OS fix a process's address space at one physical location forever?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)
cards.answer: Multiple processes are being run and swapped in and out of physical memory over time, and each one thinks it owns address zero, so the OS needs the freedom to place (and later move) a process's data anywhere in physical RAM without the process's own code having to change.

cards.prompt: Conventionally, the heap is drawn growing ___ from just above the code and static data, while the stack grows upward from the top of the address space — leaving unused space between them that either region can claim as it grows, without a fixed boundary between them.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)

cards.prompt: Conventionally, the heap is drawn growing downward from just above the code and static data, while the stack grows ___ from the top of the address space — leaving unused space between them that either region can claim as it grows, without a fixed boundary between them.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)

cards.prompt: Why does free() need no size argument even though malloc() does?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)
cards.answer: The allocator stores each block's size as metadata alongside the block itself (commonly just before the returned pointer), so free() can look up how much to reclaim from that bookkeeping rather than requiring the caller to remember and pass it back.

cards.prompt: A program calls `free(p)` and then, later in the same function, reads through `p` again without reallocating it. What kind of bug is this?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)

choices.text: A memory leak
A dangling pointer (use-after-free)
A double allocation
A stack overflow

cards.prompt: Explain why a long-running server process is far more vulnerable to slow memory leaks than a short command-line utility that runs once and exits, even though both have the same kind of bug in their code.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)

cards.prompt: The simplest scheme is dynamic relocation using a pair of hardware registers: the CPU has a ___ register holding where this process's memory starts in physical RAM, and a bounds register holding the size of that region. A virtual address is translated by adding that starting offset, and the hardware checks the address against the size limit first to catch out-of-range accesses.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)

cards.prompt: The simplest scheme is dynamic relocation using a pair of hardware registers: the CPU has a base register holding where this process's memory starts in physical RAM, and a ___ register holding the size of that region. A virtual address is translated by adding that starting offset, and the hardware checks the address against the size limit first to catch out-of-range accesses.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)

cards.prompt: Why is a bounds check needed even though the base register already relocates addresses?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)
cards.answer: Without a bounds check, a process could generate a virtual address larger than its own address space and, after the base is added, land inside another process's memory or unallocated physical memory — the bounds check is what turns relocation into isolation.

cards.prompt: How does segmentation avoid wasting the gap between a small heap and the stack?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)
cards.answer: Because the stack is its own segment with its own base and bounds, the OS only needs to allocate physical memory for the segments actually in use and their current sizes, not for a single contiguous span that has to cover the gap between an unrelated heap and stack.

cards.prompt: A system uses segmentation with separate code, heap, and stack segments. What new fragmentation problem does this introduce that plain base-and-bounds did not have?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)

choices.text: Internal fragmentation within a single segment
External fragmentation across free chunks of physical memory
Fragmentation of the CPU's register file
Fragmentation only affects the code segment

cards.prompt: Explain why a bounds violation should trap into the OS rather than the hardware simply refusing the access silently — what does the OS need to do with that information?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)

cards.prompt: Free-space allocators commonly track free chunks with a ___, a linked structure threaded through the free chunks themselves — each free chunk's header doubles as a list node, which is why free chunks need to be at least large enough to hold that header.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)

cards.prompt: Why does best fit, despite its name, often perform worse in practice than it sounds like it should?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)
cards.answer: Best fit tends to leave behind many tiny, barely-usable leftover slivers (the chunk chosen is only just big enough, so the remainder after splitting is often too small to satisfy future requests), and a full linear scan of the free list to find the best chunk is also slow.

cards.prompt: What operation reverses splitting, and why does an allocator need to perform it?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)
cards.answer: Coalescing merges two adjacent free chunks back into one larger free chunk when a block is freed and it happens to sit next to another already-free block; without coalescing, a system could accumulate many small, adjacent free fragments that could have combined into a block big enough for a large future request.

cards.prompt: Fragmentation itself comes in two distinct flavors worth keeping apart. ___ fragmentation is space wasted inside an allocated chunk because it is bigger than what was requested (as buddy allocation's rounding causes), while external fragmentation is space wasted between allocated chunks, scattered across many free fragments none of which individually fits the next request.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)

cards.prompt: An allocator uses buddy allocation. A caller requests 12KB from a system where blocks are always powers of two. What is the main cost of this scheme?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)

choices.text: External fragmentation from scattered chunk sizes
Internal fragmentation from rounding requests up to the next power of two
O(n) search time through the whole free list
Inability to ever coalesce freed memory

cards.prompt: Explain why external fragmentation cannot be fully solved just by choosing a cleverer placement strategy (best fit, worst fit, first fit) among fixed free chunks, and what compaction would have to do instead.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)

cards.prompt: The hardware provides two privilege levels. In ___, code cannot directly issue privileged instructions (like ones that touch disk or reconfigure the MMU) — attempting one causes the hardware to trap into the OS instead. In kernel mode, the OS itself runs with full access to the hardware. A process's normal code always runs at that lower privilege level.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

cards.prompt: The hardware provides two privilege levels. In user mode, code cannot directly issue privileged instructions (like ones that touch disk or reconfigure the MMU) — attempting one causes the hardware to trap into the OS instead. In ___, the OS itself runs with full access to the hardware. A process's normal code always runs at that lower privilege level.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

cards.prompt: How does a user-mode process ask the OS to perform a privileged operation, such as reading a file?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: It executes a system call, a special trap instruction; the trap saves the caller's register state and jumps to a fixed, OS-defined entry point in kernel mode, so the process cannot jump into arbitrary kernel code, only through the sanctioned entry.

cards.prompt: Why must only the OS be allowed to configure the trap table, and never a user process?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: If a user process could set the trap handler address, it could point a system call trap at its own code and have that code run with full kernel privilege, defeating the entire protection scheme.

cards.prompt: A single trap into the kernel isn't enough to keep control forever, though — a process could simply never make a system call and monopolize the CPU. The classic fix is a ___: hardware raises an interrupt at a fixed interval regardless of what the process is doing, forcing a trap back into the OS, which can then decide whether to keep running this process or switch to another. This is what makes preemptive scheduling possible without cooperation from the program being interrupted.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

cards.prompt: A process is running an infinite loop with no system calls and no I/O. What lets the OS regain control of the CPU?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

choices.text: The process's next system call
The scheduler polling the process's state
A periodic timer interrupt forcing a trap into the OS
The compiler inserting yield calls automatically

cards.prompt: Why does "return-from-trap" not necessarily resume the same process that trapped into the kernel?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: Between the trap and the return, the OS's scheduler is free to swap in a different process's saved register state, so the trap and the eventual return-from-trap can belong to two different processes even though they are the same hardware instruction pair.

cards.prompt: Explain why direct execution alone (running a program straight on the CPU with no traps or timer interrupts) is unsafe for a multiprogrammed OS, even though it is the fastest possible way to run code.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

cards.prompt: The base rules: a higher-priority queue always runs before a lower one, and jobs on the same queue share the CPU in round robin. To decide how priority changes over time, MLFQ tracks a job's ___: the amount of CPU time it may use at its current priority level before being demoted one queue.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)

cards.prompt: Why does a job entering the system start at the highest-priority queue rather than the lowest?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)
cards.answer: The scheduler has no information yet about whether the job is short and interactive or long and CPU-bound, so it optimistically assumes short/interactive first; a truly short job finishes quickly from there, while a long job reveals itself by using up its allotment and sinking down.

cards.prompt: How can a process game a naive MLFQ that resets allotment on voluntary yield?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)
cards.answer: The process can issue a near-instant I/O request just before its allotment runs out, over and over, so it never gets demoted despite consuming nearly all of the CPU's time — it "relinquishes" just often enough to stay parked at the top queue.

cards.prompt: What mechanism keeps a long-running, low-priority MLFQ job from starving?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)
cards.answer: A periodic priority boost: after a fixed time period S, every job in the system — regardless of current queue — is moved back to the topmost queue, giving starved long-running jobs a fresh chance to run again.

cards.prompt: The priority-boost interval S is set far too long for the workload. What is the most likely symptom?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)

choices.text: Long-running jobs starve for extended stretches before being boosted
Short jobs never get to run at all
The scheduler degenerates into pure FIFO immediately
Context-switch overhead disappears entirely

cards.prompt: Explain why MLFQ counts as "learning from history to predict the future," and describe one way that strategy can backfire if a job's behavior changes partway through its life.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)

cards.prompt: Why do multi-level page tables use less memory than a single-level table?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)
cards.answer: An entire region of the address space that is unused doesn't need its second-level page table allocated at all — the page directory entry for that region can simply be marked invalid, so memory is only spent on page-table chunks that actually cover pages the process is using.

cards.prompt: Swapping extends virtual memory beyond what physical RAM can hold, by using disk (or, in modern systems, flash) as a backing store for pages that don't currently fit in RAM. The OS designates a region of the disk as ___, and a page not currently resident in physical memory is instead written out there.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)

cards.prompt: What happens on a page fault for a valid page currently swapped out to disk?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)
cards.answer: The OS's page-fault handler reads the page's location from the PTE, finds (or evicts something to make) a free physical frame, reads the page's contents in from disk into that frame, updates the PTE to point at the new frame and mark it present, and then retries the faulting instruction.

cards.prompt: Why do real systems use the clock algorithm instead of exact LRU?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)
cards.answer: Exact LRU would require updating bookkeeping on every memory reference, which is far too costly to do at hardware speed; the clock algorithm instead relies on a cheap hardware-set "use" bit per page and periodic sweeps, trading precision for something actually affordable to run.

cards.prompt: Physical memory is nearly full and every running process's active pages together exceed it. What is this condition called?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)

choices.text: Internal fragmentation
A TLB miss storm
Thrashing
Priority inversion

cards.prompt: Explain why the optimal page-replacement policy (evict what's used furthest in the future) is useful even though no real OS can implement it directly.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)

cards.prompt: A virtual address is split into a ___ (VPN), which selects an entry in the process's page table, and a page offset, which is left unchanged by translation because it just locates a byte within the page — only the page number needs to be translated, not the offset.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))

cards.prompt: Why does a page table need a valid bit, given sparse address spaces?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: Most address spaces are sparse (a small amount of used memory in a huge virtual range), so allocating a PTE only marks pages actually in use as valid; an access to an unmapped page's still-present-but-invalid PTE traps to the OS instead of silently succeeding against garbage.

cards.prompt: What hardware structure avoids a full page-table walk on every memory access?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: The TLB (translation lookaside buffer), a small hardware cache of recently used virtual-to-physical page translations sitting inside (or next to) the CPU; a TLB hit supplies the frame number in one cycle, skipping the memory access to the page table entirely.

cards.prompt: Who refills a TLB entry after a miss on a software-managed TLB, and how?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: The OS does: the hardware traps into a miss handler, which walks the OS's own page-table structure and installs the new translation using privileged instructions, then the faulting instruction is retried.

cards.prompt: Why does switching between processes risk invalidating the TLB's cached entries?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: TLB entries map virtual addresses to physical frames for one specific address space, so after a context switch the previous process's cached translations are meaningless (or, worse, wrong) for the new process's virtual addresses, unless the TLB tags entries with a process/address-space id to keep multiple processes' translations valid at once.

cards.prompt: A process has excellent temporal locality but the TLB is very small relative to its working set. What is the most likely consequence?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))

choices.text: Frequent TLB misses forcing repeated page-table walks
The page table itself becomes unnecessary
Internal fragmentation increases sharply
The valid bit is checked less often

cards.prompt: Explain why fixed-size pages eliminate external fragmentation compared to segmentation, and what kind of fragmentation paging can still leave behind.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))

cards.prompt: The OS tracks a process's status internally, typically as one of three states: it is ___ when its instructions are actually executing on a CPU, ready when it could run but the OS has chosen another process instead, and blocked when it cannot run until some event (such as an I/O completion) occurs, even if a CPU is free.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)

cards.prompt: The OS tracks a process's status internally, typically as one of three states: it is running when its instructions are actually executing on a CPU, ___ when it could run but the OS has chosen another process instead, and blocked when it cannot run until some event (such as an I/O completion) occurs, even if a CPU is free.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)

cards.prompt: The OS tracks a process's status internally, typically as one of three states: it is running when its instructions are actually executing on a CPU, ready when it could run but the OS has chosen another process instead, and ___ when it cannot run until some event (such as an I/O completion) occurs, even if a CPU is free.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)

cards.prompt: Why can't a blocked process simply be given the CPU when it becomes the highest-priority job?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: A blocked process is waiting on an event outside the CPU's control (e.g., a disk read); running it would not make progress, so the OS leaves it off the ready pool until the event fires and moves it to ready.

cards.prompt: Why does fork() return a different value in the parent than in the child?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: fork() returns the child's process ID to the parent and 0 to the child, so the same post-fork code can branch on the return value to run different logic in each process even though both start from the identical point in the program.

cards.prompt: Why split process creation into fork() then exec() instead of one spawn call?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: Splitting them lets the shell run code between the fork and the exec, in the child only — for example redirecting a file descriptor or setting up a pipe — before the child's image is replaced by the target program, which a single combined call could not support.

cards.prompt: A parent calls `wait()` right after `fork()`. What is the parent waiting for?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)

choices.text: The child to call exec()
The child to terminate, so the parent can reap its exit status
The scheduler to grant the parent another time slice
The child to release its file descriptors

cards.prompt: Explain why an OS needs `wait()` at all — what would go wrong for the parent, or for the system's process table, if a parent never collected a terminated child's exit status?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)

cards.prompt: Lottery scheduling implements this with randomness. Each job holds some number of ___, and on every scheduling decision the scheduler draws a random winning ticket and runs whichever job holds it — a job with twice as many as another wins (and thus runs) about twice as often, in expectation, over many draws.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)

cards.prompt: Why is lottery scheduling only probabilistically fair over short intervals?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: Because the winner is chosen by drawing a random ticket each time, short runs can deviate from the target ratio purely by chance (e.g., a low-ticket job could win several draws in a row); the guarantee only holds as a long-run average, by the law of large numbers.

cards.prompt: Which job does stride scheduling pick to run next?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: The scheduler always picks whichever runnable job currently has the lowest accumulated pass value, then adds that job's stride to its pass value — since a high-ticket job's stride is small, its pass value climbs slowly, so it gets picked more often.

cards.prompt: Linux's CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) takes a related but distinct approach: instead of tickets, it tracks each runnable process's ___, virtual runtime, which increases as the process consumes CPU time, and always runs whichever runnable process currently has the lowest such value — approximating an ideal where every process's virtual runtime advances at the same rate.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)

cards.prompt: How does CFS use "nice" values to give some processes a larger share of the CPU than others?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: A process's nice value sets a weight that scales how fast its vruntime accumulates per unit of real CPU time — a higher-priority (lower nice) process's vruntime grows more slowly for the same work, so it appears to have run "less" and gets picked again sooner.

cards.prompt: Two jobs run under lottery scheduling: A has 100 tickets, B has 300 tickets (400 total). What is B's expected long-run share of the CPU?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)

choices.text: 100%, since it holds the most tickets

cards.prompt: Explain why stride scheduling can reproduce lottery scheduling's target ratios with far less short-term variance, given that both are driven by the same underlying ticket counts.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)

cards.prompt: Why can a scheduler that is excellent for turnaround time be terrible for response time?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)
cards.answer: Optimizing turnaround favors running whichever job finishes soonest to completion without interruption, but that can force an interactive job to wait behind a long job's entire run before it is ever touched, producing a long response time even though total turnaround looks good on average.

cards.prompt: What is the "convoy effect" in FIFO scheduling?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)
cards.answer: A short, quick job gets queued behind a long-running job that arrived slightly earlier, so many short jobs collectively wait on one long one, inflating average turnaround time well beyond what the jobs' own lengths would justify.

cards.prompt: Why does an overly short RR time slice hurt performance despite better response time?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)
cards.answer: A very short time slice means the fixed cost of a context switch (saving and restoring register state, flushing caches/TLB entries) happens far more often relative to useful work done, so switching overhead starts to dominate and total throughput drops.
